summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds including sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives that guarantee effect through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. There is no criminalisation of trans identity or expression. Male same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1994 and the Constitutional Court struck down the common-law offences of sodomy and unnatural sexual act in 1998.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which allows a person to change their sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports reflecting their gender identity. Surgery is not required, but medical evidence is, typically hormone replacement therapy, which is available from age 16, with surgery permitted from 18 or younger with parental consent. The requirements pathologise identity and, because the statute recognises only a binary change of sex status, non-binary people cannot obtain a marker matching their identity. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African identity documents, the first such move on the continent, with an internal identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents; a departmental policy official confirmed the change would take a few years as it moves through consultation to legislation, and no such marker is in issue at the time of writing.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for a transgender inmate, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena, against the Department of Correctional Services in case 2024/070075. The court held that refusing a transgender prisoner the gender-affirming health care prescribed for her falls below the required standard of health care, and likewise condemned the refusal to allow feminising clothing and accessories. Orders compel the department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. Lawyers for Human Rights, which brought the case, and the South African Human Rights Commission, acting through the national preventive mechanism, both welcomed the ruling as binding on correctional facilities.

Earlier reporting had established that the department maintains a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but that rights organisations doubted it was being implemented in practice. Health-care access outside custody is uneven: in December 2024 LGBTI rights organisation OUT LGBT Well-being reported that activists in East London had submitted a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Private gender-affirming care is largely urban and expensive, and public systems face long waits, which forces people from rural areas to travel to major cities.

Facility access remains contested. A 2024 academic analysis in the Potchefstroom Electronic Law Journal examined whether gender-segregated bathrooms that exclude transgender and non-binary people constitute unfair discrimination under PEPUDA read with the Constitution, and concluded that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access.

Violence against visibly trans and gender-nonconforming people is a documented risk. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left severe facial injuries; an arrest was subsequently reported. OUT LGBT Well-being counted five LGBTI murders in December 2024 alone. Activists and researchers document lesbians and trans people being beaten, murdered and subjected to so-called corrective rape, and accuse police of negligent handling of cases, including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013; ActionAid has condemned the resulting impunity. Abuse also reaches routine state contact: Gender Dynamix reported in 2024 that a trans woman was denied the right to file a domestic-violence case after showing her identity document, amid police mockery, and trans people describe mismatched documents exposing them to humiliation, refusal of service and threats of arrest for fraud.

Protection machinery exists alongside that record. The Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024, signed in May 2024 after passage through both houses of Parliament, explicitly lists sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression-related grounds and sex characteristics among protected characteristics; its hate-speech offence requires a clear intention to be harmful, to incite harm or to promote hatred. Human Rights Watch and other legal commentators argued the Act is vague and threatening to freedom of expression. Earlier instruments include the Department of Justice National Task Team, established in 2011, and the National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities of April 2014, which addressed sex- and gender-based violence and provided a rapid response team for unsolved cases, and a violence-prevention programme launched by then Justice Minister Jeff Radebe in the early 2010s.

Partner recognition is settled: the Civil Union Act of 2006 permits same-sex unions, and court decisions before and after it extended immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption to same-sex couples. Conversion therapy on children is not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005; a bill introduced in 2021 would ban it, introduced after three teenagers aged 15 to 19 died at a conversion therapy camp whose operators were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015.

Public opinion is comparatively favourable but sharply uneven. A 2017 ILGA poll found 67% backing equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people, while the same poll found 24% still favoured charging people in same-sex relationships as criminals. Afrobarometer recorded in 2016 that 67% would be comfortable with a same-sex couple as neighbours, against a 21% continental average, and an Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% supporting some legal recognition for same-sex couples. Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships bear disproportionate violence.
tangentialFactors:
South Africa ranks among the strongest performers internationally on the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and the Equaldex LGBT Equality Index, and the official South African Tourism website publishes travel guidance aimed at gay and lesbian visitors. Index placement reflects law on the books and does not measure enforcement quality or violence risk at street level.

Pride has been held in Johannesburg since the first Lesbian and Gay Pride march on 13 October 1990, and marches now run in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Pretoria and Soweto, with smaller events in towns including Knysna, whose Pink Loerie festival draws visitors nationally. Cape Town has an established gay village around De Waterkant, a permanent rainbow crosswalk and a Pink Lane.

Historical context matters for expectations of state hostility: under the National Party, male same-sex conduct carried up to seven years' imprisonment and was used to break up gay events, as in the January 1966 Forest Town raid. A 1969 amendment to the Immorality Act barred men from erotic conduct with more than two people present, and a residual provision kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts against 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act equalised it in 2007; the inequality was declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v National Director of Public Prosecutions in 2008 with retroactive effect to 27 April 1994. In 2012 the Contralesa organisation petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution and was rejected by the ANC parliamentary caucus.

One adjacent health rule is worth noting for its neutrality: the South African National Blood Service required men who have sex with men to abstain for six months before donating until 2014, when it was replaced by a gender-neutral rule barring any donor with a new sexual partner in the previous six months or more than one partner in that period.
localsOnly:
Residents who want a marker change must satisfy the medical requirements of the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, which typically means documented hormone replacement therapy. The Act's binary framing means non-binary residents have no route to a matching marker, and the gender-neutral identity document announced by the Department of Home Affairs in October 2021 had not been legislated at the time of writing.

Prison conditions for trans residents are governed by the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure, which the Gauteng High Court ordered the department to enforce in November 2025 alongside orders for state-funded hormone treatment and gender-expression clothing. Monitoring of compliance falls to the department, with oversight roles for the South African Human Rights Commission and organisations such as Lawyers for Human Rights.

Residents seeking gender-affirming care face a two-tier system: private treatment is concentrated in cities and is costly, while public facilities carry long waiting lists. Eastern Cape activists documented year-long delays at Frere Hospital in East London in December 2024. Trans minors can access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent.

Young trans and non-binary South Africans also contend with a bullying environment that has no specific anti-bullying statute, though the Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011 and the Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 cover homophobic harassment and youth offending. A 2015 TIMSS survey found 44% of Grade 5 pupils bullied weekly and 34% monthly, the highest of 38 countries, with Grade 9 pupils third-most bullied at 17% weekly. Conversion therapy remains lawful for children; a 2021 bill to prohibit it had not been enacted at the time of writing.

LGBTI student organisations operate at Wits, the University of Cape Town, Stellenbosch, the University of Johannesburg and the University of the Western Cape.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory describes border checks, passport control or entry screening of travellers to South Africa, so the treatment of trans visitors at ports of entry, including any scanning or secondary questioning triggered by mismatched documents, is unresolved here. The closest sourced parallel is domestic: documented incidents of trans people being refused service or threatened with arrest over identity documents that do not match presentation.

The sources do not record whether the November 2025 Equality Court orders against the Department of Correctional Services have been complied with, or whether any appeal was noted, so enforcement of those remedies for a detained trans person is unresolved.

The status of the 2021 bill banning conversion therapy on children, and of the Department of Home Affairs' gender-neutral identification plans announced in October 2021, is stated in the sources only up to the point of introduction and consultation respectively; final enactment is not documented here.

Whether the 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act has produced prosecutions involving gender identity as a hate-crime aggravator is not sourced. The inventory documents the Act's commencement and its protected grounds, not its case law.
